title: Reduced Relative Clauses
subtitle: Shorten a relative clause by dropping the pronoun and using a participle.
objectives: Reduce an active relative clause using the -ing form
Reduce a passive relative clause using the past participle
Recognize when a relative clause can and can't be reduced

content.intro: Now that you're comfortable with who/which/that, let's make your writing tighter and more natural by dropping the relative pronoun when possible.

rules.heading: a) Active clauses → -ing form
rules.body:
When the relative pronoun is the subject of an active verb, drop "who/which/that" + the verb, and use the -ing form instead.

  • The man who is standing there is my uncle. → The man standing there is my uncle.
  • People who live in cities often complain about noise. → People living in cities often complain about noise.

rules.heading: b) Passive clauses → past participle
rules.body:
• The book which was written by Tolkien is a classic. → The book written by Tolkien is a classic.
  • The car that was damaged in the accident has been repaired. → The car damaged in the accident has been repaired.

rules.heading: c) When you can't reduce
rules.body: You can't reduce when the relative pronoun is the object, not the subject: "The book that I read" cannot become "The book reading" — there's no subject relationship to reduce.

examples: The man standing there is my uncle.
People living in cities often complain about noise.
The book written by Tolkien is a classic.
The car damaged in the accident has been repaired.
The woman sitting next to me is a doctor.
Documents signed before the deadline will be accepted.

commonMistakes.wrong: The man standed there is my uncle.
commonMistakes.right: The man standing there is my uncle.
commonMistakes.why: Active reduced clauses use the -ing form, not the past tense.

commonMistakes.wrong: The book writing by Tolkien is a classic.
commonMistakes.right: The book written by Tolkien is a classic.
commonMistakes.why: Passive reduced clauses use the past participle (written), not the -ing form.

commonMistakes.wrong: The book reading is on the table. (meaning: the book that I am reading)
commonMistakes.right: The book that I am reading is on the table.
commonMistakes.why: You can't reduce a clause where the pronoun is the object — there's no active/passive subject relationship here.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Reduce each relative clause using the -ing form or the past participle.

items.prompt: The woman ___ (sit) next to me is a doctor.
The car ___ (damage) in the accident has been repaired.
Students ___ (study) hard usually get good grades.
Emails ___ (send) after 6pm are answered the next day.
The report ___ by the team is ready for review.
items.explanation: The team prepared it — passive relationship — past participle.

items.prompt: People ___ in this building must show ID.
items.explanation: The people work here — active relationship — -ing form.

items.incorrect: The letter wrote by my grandmother is very old.
answer: The letter written by my grandmother is very old.
items.explanation: Passive reduced clauses need the past participle (written), not the simple past form (wrote).

items.incorrect: The man wait outside is my brother.
answer: The man waiting outside is my brother.
items.explanation: Active reduced clauses need the -ing form.

summary: Active relative clause → drop the pronoun + verb, use -ing.
Passive relative clause → drop the pronoun + "was/were", use the past participle.
You can only reduce when the relative pronoun is the subject of its clause.
